On section 2-Right to marry again.
Mr. WOODSWORTH':	I should like to
ask what the effect of this section really is. If I understand the matter aright, the solemnization of marriage is entirely a provincial matter. Both in the province of Ontario and in the province of Quebec, it is placed in the hands of the clergymen of the various religious bodies. We are told that certain churches in this country are opposed to divorce and refuse to allow remarriage. That means that a large number of clergymen both in the province of Ontario and Quebec absolutely refuse to conduct a marriage ceremony where the parties have been divorced. I take it that that means that those clergymen refuse to be bound by the findings of this parliament. We give the right to the innocent party to remarry, and by inference that right is given also to the other party, but certain clergymen refuse to be bound by the decision of this house. They set themselves up as being superior to parliament and refuse to permit the marriage of those people who this parliament say may be remarried. Perhaps it may be a theoretical question as to which is supreme, parliament or the church, but there is a practical aspect to this matter. As I have said, the solemnization of marriage in these two provinces is left in the hands of the officials of the various churches. In practice, that means that it is very, very difficult to seeure a clergyman in Ontario or Quebec who is willing to remarry divorced people. It is possible in Great Britain for divorced people to be remarried before a justice of the peace. I do not know whether that is possible in any of our provinces, but it certainly is not possible in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec from which most of these cases originate.

You cannot be married by
a justice of the peace in Great Britain.
By a magistrate.
You can marry much easier than that in Scotland.

I think I am
correct, Mr. Chairman, when I say that there is a provision in Great Britain for civil marriage.

I accept the correction. but the point I was trying to make is that there is provision for civil marriage. I am told that in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec there is no provision for civil marriage, which means that these people will have to go to a clergyman to be remarried and since a great many of the religious bodies are opposed to the marriage of divorced people it will mean, as far as these two provinces are concerned, that this clause 2 amounts to very little. The person who has been given the right to remarry will have to go up and down the country in an endeavour to find a clergyman who will consent to perform the marriage ceremony. I raise this point simply because it reveals a very anomalous situation in that this parliament is given distinct jurisdiction over marriage and divorce while the provinces have jurisdiction over the solemnization of marriage.

Mr. Chairman, my well
founded opinion, after many years in parliament, is that at least one-half or three-quarters of these applications would not 'be made if this second clause was not included in the bill. It has always been my opinion that a grave injustice is done by placing the guilty party upon the same footing as the innocent party. It is bad enough to give the innocent party power to remarry without giving the same power to the other party. As regards the religious law, if members of the Roman Catholic church want to comply with its rules and regulations, that church does not permit the remarriage of divorced people. The church of England in Canada has also made it known that it will not allow the remarriage of divorced people. There is good authority for that point of view in the Bible if those who are interested would only read the words of our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ. I hold that these churches are not governed, so far as their rules and regulations are concerned, by any decision of parliament. The religious authority is quite independent of the civil authority, and while the civil authority has complete jurisdiction within its own domain, in the religious domain each church is quite independent of parliament. I regret once more that parliament is allowing such a large number of divorce bills to go through, over three hundred of them, without full evidence, because the two parties have not been heard. We are giving a decision on ex parte evidence and I am glad to see that in the province of Ontario, where the great majority of these
applications come from, there is a movement looking to a change in the procedure so that the power of granting divorces may be taken away altogether from the Dominion parliament.
Section agreed to
Bill reported, read the third time and passed on division.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF CONVENTION TO MARINE AND FISHERIES COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has been intimated to
the government that some hon. members of the house would like to have detailed information with respect to this treaty. In order to supply the information which they wish to have, it would appear to be desirable to have the resolution referred to an appropriate committee of the house where that information could be given. In the form in which the motion stands, it being a motion to approve a convention, nothing more is contemplated than formal approval after consideration of the resolution by this house while the Speaker is in the chair; it is not contemplated to have the resolution as it stands referred to the committee of the whole house. In the circumstances, believing that the select standing committee on marine and fisheries is perhaps the best committee to deal with this particular convention, I move:
That the subject matter of the government notice of motion standing on the order of proceedings for this day respecting the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries in the Fraser river system- be referred to the select standing committee on marine and fisheries.
Among other advantages of having the resolution so referred is that of enabling the committee to hear at first hand from the officers of the department who have had to do with the negotiation of the treaty itself.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF CONVENTION TO MARINE AND FISHERIES COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the course suggested by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is one which commends itself to our judgment for it affords an opportunity for detailed consideration of the merits of the treaty that might otherwise be denied, and I have great pleasure in supporting the motion that has just been made.
While I am on my feet may I venture to suggest to the right hon. the Prime Minister, as indeed I have already done, that he consider the propriety of approving a treaty of this character by legislation rather than by resolution. I shall not discuss that at this moment, but I think if he will look into it he will satisfy himself that this form of treaty which in its substance involves future legislation should be approved itself by an act of parliament. I have gathered together some of the authorities, and I shall be glad ' at a future time to give them to the right hon. gentleman. I think myself that the matter should be dealt with by a substantive bill and not by a mere resolution.

He said: Mr. Speaker, as you have just indicated in reading the resolution, this protocol was signed at Geneva in June, 1925-signed,
I understand, by some thirty-four different countries, including Great Britain and Canada. The protocol has since been ratified by a number of countries, but has not been ratified by either Great Britain or Canada.
At the meeting of the preparatory commission on disarmament which was held at Geneva this spring, Lord Cushendun, on behalf of His Majesty's government in Great Britain, intimated that it was the intention of His Majesty's government in Great Britain to ratify the protocol, subject to two reservations, the first being that its provisions should bind only vis-a-vis such countries as are also parties to the protocol; and the second being

We instructed our representative on the preparatory commission on disarmament, Mr. Riddell, to inform the commission that it was the intention of the Dominion government to ask the approval of parliament to the protocol in order that it might be ratified at the same time on behalf of Canada as it is ratified on behalf of His Majesty's government in Great Britain. It is for that reason that the house is now being asked to approve the protocol. I do not think it necessary to go into the provisions of the protocol. speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subsubtopic: PROHIBITION OF POISONOUS GASES AND BACTERIOLOGICAL METHODS OF WARFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the precedent
has just been set in the previous resolution of reference to the most appropriate committee. Several years ago at the Prime Minister's own suggestion the committee on industrial relations was enlarged to be the committee on industrial and international relations. I think during the four or five years' existence of that committee there has never been any reference to it of any international matter. It strikes me that it would be highly desirable that the committee, and through the committee the house at large, should be more closely in touch with international affairs. In the past we in Canada have had very little to do with international affairs, and it is desirable that the general public should be familiarized more or less with the details and the implications of our international relations.
In order that this be accomplished I can see no better way than the discussing of these relationships in this house by going into details in regard to such matters before a committee, as is done with regard to other matters. Hence, since we have just referred the previous resolution to a committee, I would venture to suggest to the Prime Minister that similar action might be taken in this case.
Further, it seems to me 'that some time, either now or later, the Prime Minister ought to give us some reason for including in this protocol certain reservations. The only reason hitherto suggested is that Great Britain has done so. I do not think that is quite enough for us. It does seem to me that we ought to have some underlying reasons of our own for such action. It may be that Great Britain in this respect is right; and' it may be that Great Britain is not right. The present policy of the British government is the policy of the Conservative party in Great Britain. I do not know why this government should necessarily follow the policy of the Conservative party of Great Britain. And in any case I think it is right that we should have definitely set before us the reasons for placing these reservations in this protocol.
I offer my previous suggestion to the Prime Minister in the hope that in this way we may gradually enter upon a better understanding of our foreign relationships.

Mr. Speaker, I heartily concur
in the observations made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this is a purely formal matter. There is nothing in this protocol that can be said to be contentious. ' We are endeavouring to prevent a form of warfare, if the world ever again should know war, which we hope it maj not, that has met with the universal reprobation of mankind. Asphyxiating and chemical gases we know wrought great havoc in the armies engaged in the last world conflict, and in one instance, which was well authenticated, use of bacteriological methods brought great disaster to a very large community. We are merely declaring in that with other nations of the world we will not have anything to do with that kind of warfare. I cannot see that there would be any use in referring this resolution to a committee, with due deference to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). Certainly there is no analogy between this and the other resolution on the order paper.
Geneva Protocol

With respect to the reservations, I apprehend that the reservations suggested by Lord Cushendun on behalf of Great Britain were reservations that were made as a result of the experience of Great Britain in the recent war. It was said that one of the greatest soldiers of the British Empire, as well as one of the great soldiers of one of the overseas dominions, was of the opinion that notwithstanding the fact that the enemy used poisonous gases,-the allies should not do so; but ultimately that judgment was over-borne and recourse was had by the armies of Great Britain and the allies to the use of poisonous gases to combat the poisonous gases used by the enemy. Large quantities of such gases were made on this continent and sent to the field of hostilties.
All that I understand these reservations to mean is that in the event of one of the parties to this protocol being engaged in hostilities and breaking the terms of the obligations, and utilizing asphyxiating or poisonous gases or bacteriological methods of warfare, we would thereby be relieved from our obligations with respect to that country, and that country only. That is, there is no general release from our dbligations, but only from those obligations that affect that party which has already broken its obligations under the protocol. That is how I understand it.

Frankly, I am all in favour of any treaty or any undertaking between nations which will eliminate the use of chemical gases. Indeed, I would go further than the Prime Minister and would propose the elimination of all means of warfare-all of them, as an hon. member suggests. Frankly, I should be agreeable to that so far as Canada is concerned. I think we have the least to fear of any nation, and we are in a geographical position of the most extraordinary advantage as compared with other nations in that regard. I have just a word or two to say,
first, with regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that the matter be referred to the committee. The provisions of the protocol now before the house contain Canada's stated and considered policy since at least 1922. In 1922, at the time of the Washington naval conference, Canada became a party to a treaty framed practically in the same terms as this, and which I understand was ratified at that time. This treaty goes further only in two respects. In the first place, it includes other parties not present at the Washington conference; as the Prime Minister indicated, it includes thirty nations. In the second place, it adds bacteriological means of warfare to those already prohibited by the Washington treaty. The special provision in the Washington treaty was article V:
The use in war of asphyxiating, poisonous or other gases, and all analogous liquids, materials or devices, having been justly condemned by the general opinion of the civilized world and a prohibition of such use having been declared in treaties to which a majority of the civilized powers aire parties.	_
The signatory powers, to the end that this prohibition shall be universally accepted as a part of international law binding alike the conscience and practice of nations, declare their assent to such prohibition, agree to be bound thereby as between themselves and invite all other civilized nations to adhere thereto.
As has been said on both sides of the house, this is no new policy for Canada, and I submit that it does not involve any technical examination which would require reference of the matter to a committee.
Secondly on the point mentioned by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) with regard to the necessity for inquiring into the good faith of the various parties to the treaty, if that suggestion is valid in respect to this treaty, how much further would1 the hon. gentleman's argument carry him in connection with the so-called Briand-Kellogg pact?

It would mean the complete examination of the defence forces, of the armaments, and of every means for warlike preparation possessed by every nation which has signed the pact. I understand that the very heart of that treaty and, I believe, the very spirit of this one, is dependence upon the good faith of the contracting parties; there are no securities either in that treaty or in this one. There is no provision as to anything that will take the place of what is prohibited, there is nothing that provides any guarantee that the terms of the treaty will be carried out. There is simply the word, the good
faith of the nations who have signed the treaty. It seems to me, therefore, that we should be flying directly in the face of these treaties, questioning the very spirit in which they were entered into, if we began immediately questioning the good faith of the parties by instituting an enquiry as to whether they intend to carry out their obligations and whether they are making preparations which might be suspected to permit of a violation at the first opportunity of the principles of the treaty.
With regard to the situation in Canada, may I say one word. Canada is not making any provision for the use of chemicals in warfare except in a defensive way. Training has been extremely limited. We have regarded the obligation imposed in the Washington treaty as our Obligation and have endeavoured to carry it out not only in spirit but in actual practice. There are in Canada at the present time probably one thousand anti-gas masks, used for the purpose of training our personnel in anti-gas measures. We have no personnel whatever engaged in connection with research, nor have we any personnel engaged in connection with the manufacture of this means of warfare. And that is the policy which we propose to carry out. The personnel we have specially trained in this work comprises one officer and two non-commissioned officers trained in England who from time to time give instructions to a limited number who in turn qualify for instructors in anti-gas measures, and I trust that will be found to be the only necessity which Canada will have to meet in that respect

It is, of course, very difficult to differentiate between chemicals used for industrial and for military purposes respectively; it is extremely difficult. The nation which has great transportation systems in connection with civilian activities is obviously better prepared for quick mobilization for war and in the same way a nation engaged in the manufacture of chemicals for purely civilian purposes, may in case of war be the quickest to adapt these agemees to military uses. We know there are developments in chemistry throughout the world, and particularly in industrial chemistry. That always can be associated with the possibility of utilizing

such gases or chemical substances in connection with war. The department with which I am connected naturally must keep before it information which we get from time to time with regard to these developments, not in any critical or suspicious sense but simply with the idea of providing defensive measures should these agencies be used by any nation which is not a party to this treaty.
While I am on my feet I would like to refer to one point in reference to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with regard to the reservations. I think that question has been dealt with already; the reservations are two. First there is a limitation that this treaty only applies as between us and similarly contracting parties; in other words the treaty is reciprocal, and in the second place we are not bound as against any enemy state who fails or whose allies fail to respect the agreement. I think that is a reasonable provision; I think the house will recognize the force of it and -necessity for it, and I do not think it is a reservation which need be submitted to a committee or, with all deference to my hon. friend, which will require very much debate in this house.

I
would like to make just one observation, and it is this: Any country might be conscientiously and sincerely intending to live up to a treaty such as this while at the same time they are going thoroughly into the manufacture of poisonous gases or bacteriological methods of warfare. In the last war, for example, without being part of a treaty it was well understood among the civilized nations that such things as poisonous gases would not be used, yet they were used to the horror and disgust of the allies at least. In the same way, in the next war, should such an unfortunate event occur, a country desiring to live uip to this treaty to the nth degree should be prepared in case one of the other countries should take the attitude which was taken during the last war. I believe no horror could have been greater than the feeling which was engendered among the allies when poisonous gases were used against them in the last war and therefore, with all due respect to other hon. -members who have spoken, I think the fact that one of the allies might be conducting a thorough examination into these methods of warfare would not necessarily mean a lack of faith should war occur. I think that action should be taken as a defensive -precaution in case one of the opposing countries adopted that method of warfare.	.

speechtext:
I see no objection to referring this matter to a committee, because I believe in that way much information might be gained which would be advantageous to a great many people. Chemical gases are used industrially, and I believe the work being done now is of great service to the industrial world and to people in general. We had an example of the effect of poisonous gases in Cleveland just a day or two ago, and if in our schools we can proceed with the study of these gases and discover defences against them we will do a lot of good, because defence against these gases is just as important as the use of gas. No country is going to produce gases for any purpose other than defence, so I think this question could be submitted to this committee with a great deal of benefit to everyone. They will find nothing prejudicial to themselves or to any other Anglo-Saxon country, but they wiil find a great deal of research work being carried on in order to protect human life against these gases.
The information obtained during the last war has been of great benefit to the world at large; perhaps many people will condemn the use of animals in experiments of this kind, but we must remember that these experiments have for their object the protection of human life, whether in war or in industry. The other day in Cleveland it would have been of great benefit if some protective measure had been available against the effects of the poisonous gases which were released during that accident; perhaps a hundred lives might have been saved. We saved thousands of lives during the war through our knowledge of how to protect our men against the effects of a common gas which, previous to the war, was used only in industrial fields. So I see no objection whatever to the suggestion that this question should be referred to a committee; I believe a great deal of information can be obtained which will assist in the protection of human life.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not desire that the passage of this resolution should be delayed by reason of my absence, and I thought I indicated that fact before I left Ottawa.
In the first place I desire to observe that the procedure adopted in this case, in my judgment, is improper; this approval should be the subject matter of legislation and should be introduced by way of a bill and not by the method which has been adopted. A few minutes ago I directed attention to what I conceived to be the true principles which should govern in a matter of this kind, and perhaps I may refer to the authorities without taking up too much time of the house.
There is an article in the British Year Book of International Law for 1928 which summarizes the whole matter. The following appears at page 59:
Anson, writing in 1908, tells us that:
"where a treaty involves a charge upon the people, or a change in the general law of the land, it may be made, but cannot be carried into effect without the consent of parliament"; and also that
"apart from precedents relating to Indian territory, it has of recent years been thought desirable, if not necessary, that the consent of parliament should be given to the cession of territory in time of peace. Cessions made at the conclusion of peace or in course of a war, or of lands acquired by conquest or cession, for which parliament has not legislated, and for which the king has not by his own act deprived himself of the power of legislating by order in council, would seem to stand on a different footing."
The summary is as follows:
We may conclude by suggesting the following summary of the present state of British constitutional law and practice.
(1)	Treaties which for their enforcement by British courts of law require some addition to or .alteration of the existing law cannot be carried into effect without legislation. Therefore the king will not be advised to ratify them unless and until such legislation has been passed or parliament has given the necessary assurance that it will be passed. A treaty imposing on Great Britain a liability to pay money either actually (for instance, to make a loan) or contingently (for instance, to guarantee a loan), usually falls within this category, because as a rule the money could .not be raised or expended without legislation.
(2)	Treaties which modify the belligerent rights of the crown when engaged in maritime warfare will receive effect in British prize courts without legislation.

(3)	Treaties made expressly subject to the approval of parliament require its approval, which is usually given in the form of a statute.
(4)	Apart from the Indian Empire, which stands on a special footing, it is the practice, amounting probably by this time to a binding constitutional convention, for treaties involving the cession of British territory to require the approval of parliament given by a statute.
The article was written by Arnold D. McNair, C.B.E., LL.D., fellow of Gonville and Cams college and university lecturer, Cambridge, and who I believe is also the editor of the last edition of Oppenheim's International Law.
The treaty made between the United States and Canada, and which we are considering, will involve the expenditure of public moneys. One parliament should not bind or restrict the full authority of another parliament unless it be done by statute, for resolutions have no place or binding authority in the courts. One of the anomalies of our system of legislation, as has been pointed out by some commentators, is that mere resolutions are not taken notice of by the courts at all; although it may be a resolution passed by the House of Common*' and passed by the Senate as well it is not taken notice of by the courts because a law can be passed by the sovereign only with the advice and consent of the commons and senate in parliament assembled. That is, the three estates of the realm must unite to give effect and validity to legislation, but in this ca.se we have only a resolution, which, although approved by the commons and the senate, has not the force or effect of a statute. It is a resolution which contemplates a charge upon the public revenues, and therefore it comes within the purview of the first rule laid down by Professor McNair.

speechtext:
We are new at dealing
with these matters in Canada, but where we have dealt with them we have endeavored to do so by legislation. Perhaps the most important of all international documents with which we have had to do was the one in connection with the International Joint Commission, and that is the subject matter of a statute which is to be found in the annual statutes for the year in which it was passed.
Another difficulty is purely a practical one, and I submit it to the Minister of Justice as being one which will commend itself to him. When rights are affected by a treaty information regarding such treaty should be easily available to those who are interested. When the treaty is attached as a schedule to a statute

Preservation of Niagara Falls
it always appears in the statute books of the country and there is no difficulty in referring to it. For instance, the parliamentary approval of the treaty between Great Britain and France made in 1919, to which Professor McNair refers, is in these terms:
1.	The approval of parliament is hereby given to the treaty set out in the schedule to this act.
2.	This act may be cited as the Anglo-French treaty (Defence of France) Act, 1919.
That embodied the whole matter. It will be observed that the words used are "approval of," not ratification; for ratification means one of the prerogative rights of the sovereign. The approval by parliament means that sanction has been given to the treaty by the representatives of the people in the form of a bill which is the recognized procedure by which parliament expresses itself for the purpose of enabling it to be recorded as a part of its deliberations upon the statute books of the country. When parliament has expressed its approval of the treaty that treaty becomes a part of the schedule to the act.
Without going further into a matter which has been already discussed, it is sufficient for my purpose to point out that some of our treaty obligations create new obligations. To implement the obligations it will be necessary either to vote money or pass legislation. The voting of money is embodied in the supply bill, which is a legislative act, so that the principle which governs in such cases should, in my judgment, govern in this. Wherever a treaty is sought to be approved by the parliament of Canada, which consists of the Senate and the House of Commons acting with the sovereign, it should be by bill and not by resolution, for wherever the document itself contains provisions which obligate this country, as one of the high contracting parties, to discharge obligations or to do any act or thing mentioned or described in the document, that can only be given effect to through legislation, then there should be legislative approval of the treaty itself by act of parliament. When we endeavour to bind the hands of future parliaments, we cannot do so by means of resolutions, but only by acts of parliament, and, therefore, I submit that this matter should have been submitted to parliament in the form of a bill.
There is another ground upon which I desire to make a few observations, and that is this: the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) was charged with the responsibility in connection with this matter, But when the minister was considering the use and conservation of water of the Spray
lakes, which are in the Rocky mountains some distance from the Bow river and in connection with which I think the minister will agree that not even the scenic beauties of the Rocky mountains park were affected, there was such a long delay that ultimately nothing was done and recourse was had to the development of additional power at the Ghost river site on the Bow river. It happens that the city of Calgary, a portion of which I have the honour to represent, is entirely dependent upon the Bow river for its supply of hydro-electric energy. The representations as to the water in that river in the early days appear, in the light of ultimate information, to have been very inaccurate and the quantity of water fell at one time as low as 600 cubic second feet in the winter season, and the minimum flow of a river is the important thing to ascertain when one is determining the question of power development. On the other hand storage possibilities are ever present in a country such as we have in western Canada, near the Rocky mountains. It was sought thus to utilize the waters of the Spray lakes. There are those connected with the parks branch of the minister's department who believe that the scenic beauties of the park would be so marred or interfered with by the construction of a dam to enable the waters of the Spray lakes to be utilized, with a tunnel to convey the water through to the river, that the matter should not be considered. A great agitation was carried on. Many of the papers in the west joined in the attack against the power company in an urgent endeavour to protect, as they said, the scenic beauties of the parks of the west.
The Niagara falls have been known in history for, I think, something like 250 years. I believe the first measurement of the falls was taken by one of the early explorers in the seventeenth century. The falls have undoubted been gradually receding. The action of the water has been to destroy partly the falls on the Canadian side. On the United States side, where the fall is much wider, a thinner film of water has been spread over the rock and the result has been that there has not been as much erosion as on the Canadian side where the body of water is greater and its action more apparent. It has been represented by United States engineers in one of their journals that the rock on the Canadian side has receded as much as five feet a year in recent years. It seemed to me to be incredible that it should recede so great a distance, but that is the figure which has been given.

That is what I am saying. They are not parties to the treaty. Naturally the United States speaks as a nation through the treaty just as does Canada. New York is a part of the United States and Ontario is a part of Canada. We are given to believe that Ontario is satisfied with the provisions of the treaty, but there is nothing to show whether the beauties of the park or the falls are matters to be considered. The point seems to be rather that more power may be available by diverting the water over a wider area and spreading it over the Horseshoe in a thinner stream, thereby causing less erosion, so that additional pbwer will be available in Ontario and in the state of New York. It is already a matter of record that, because of this treaty, the state of New York has said to the private corporation operating on that side that while that additional water is to be available by the methods employed, they must pay to the state of New York a license fee not only for the additional water to be secured, but for water now being taken 
about which heretofore there was a grave question whether they would pay anything or not. That is a matter of record. I suggest that the principle that has governed in eastern Canada in considering this matter should also be applied in western Canada.
When the matter was actively before the department in connection with the Spray falls, I was a shareholder in the Calgary Power Company, although I was not a member of the house, When I assumed my present duties I disposed of such few shares as I had remaining in that enterprise, and therefore I feel I can speak with some degree of freedom with relation to it. It seems to me that you should not have one set of principles governing in the west where, for instance, in Calgary we are wholly dependent on that development for hydro-electrical energy, and another set in the east with respect to Niagara falls and the hydro-electric development dependent upon that large head of water.
I desire to refer to but one other matter- the method to be used is the construction of submerged dams. Mr. Isham Randolph, the elder, if I recall aright, according to a report he made, did not believe that was the best method to adopt. They had in mind at that time the creation of small islands, with sufficient loam upon them to enable some vegetation to appear so that the utilization of the water would be in harmony with the beautification of the park and the scenery surrounding the falls. The present scheme, so far as I can gather from the documents, contemplates nothing more than submerged concrete dams which will be close to the surface of the water and will not give any additional green appearance to the surrounding landscape and not add in any sense to its beautification. That at least, is the contention which has been made. I suppose the minister will say that this is a matter the details of which might be worked out by those charged with that responsibility. The treaty in the ultimate analysis is one made by the United States because of the insistence of the private power interests in the state of New York; and as regards Canada I suppose, not without the same measure of truth it may be said the treaty is largely the outcome of the representations of those who are seeking additional hydro-electrical energy in Ontario. Those are both desirable ends; both are ends to which we should try to lend our assistance in every way possible, but not if as a result the beauty of the falls is to be destroyed. If we are in any way to lessen the scenic beauty of these falls which, as I say,

Preservation of Niagara Falls
have been world renowned for over two centuries, we should not even for the purpose of getting a little additional horsepower, become parties to the transaction. It was only because of that fear which I expressed to some of my colleagues a few weeks ago, that the matter was delayed, apart altogether from the discrimination which I thought was being piactised between the east and the west in connection with this matter, scenic beauty is desirable both east and west, but the principle of utility should at least be applied in the same way in the east as in the west, and as I have said, I am firmly of opinion that the methods adopted are not those which one of the most eminent engineers of his time recommended should be applied, and departure from which will certainly detract from the scenic beauties of Niagara falls and park.
The first objection I have urged as to the method adopted is common to all these questions of the approval of treaties. We are entering upon a career of international treaties. It is highly desirable that we should settle the practice with some degree of certainty. I shall have something to say later as to section 132 of the British North America Act, which in terms does not contemplate this country making treaties with foreign countries apart from the empire. Section 132 I think should be closely studied having regard to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in determining who is a "person" within that act for the purpose of taking a seat in the senate. Having regard to the terms of that decision, it does occur to me that it is not an unfair inference to conclude that section 132 of the British North America Act should be construed by the same canons of construction. In the event of the Prime Minister considering this fall amendments necessary to the British North America Act to enable Canada to exercise powers that belong to this Dominion if we are on an equality of status with Great Britain, I would suggest that he study section 132 in order that the treaty-making powers may be properly exercised without any question being raised in the courts, as might hereafter be done, as to the true interpretation and meaning to be placed upon section 132. There is only one purpose I have so far as the first matter is concerned, and that is that our practice should be settled along the lines that are supported by precedent and reason and that will be relied upon by future parliaments and future generations as establishing a system that is sound from every standpoint. and I cannot think that any approval 78594-168
of a treaty is sound that undertakes to bind the action of future parliaments without the consent of parliament expressed in the manner and form in the constitution provided-by His Majesty the King by and with the consent of the House of Commons and Senate in parliament assembled-and not by a mere resolution of the two houses of parliament.

May I say a word or two with regard to the first point raised by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I did not know that the matter was to be brought up in this manner, and I can only rely on my memory and on what I believe to be the sound principles governing this matter. .
As my hon. friend knows, the ratifying power in matters of treaties varies with different nations. In some countries the ratification is made by parliament; in others it is made both by parliament and the king; in others it is made by one branch of parliament. In the United States, for instance, the power of ratification belongs to the senate. So far as British countries are concerned, it is His Majesty the King who ratifies the treaty. So far as the British practice is concerned, it is and it was only when money was to be expended under the treaty that the treaty was formally submitted to the imperial parliament before being ratified.

Or if it affected any vested
interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
When the Versailles
treaty of peace was submitted for approval, I remember reading a speech of Mr. Lloyd George, then Prime Minister of Great Britain, in which he reiterated that the ratification power is vested in the king, but that that treaty was of such tremendous importance that he thought it proper to submit it to the approval of parliament before asking for ratification by His Majesty the King. In this country for the last few years we have taken the stand that no treaty should be ratified before it is submitted for the approval of this parliament. That course the government has followed in every instance, and it is following it in this case. When there is need of special legislation for the purpose of enforcing a treaty, legislation has been introduced, but introduced apart from the treaty. I remember an instance in 1923 or 1924 when the halibut treaty was ratified. I was Minister of Marine and Fisheries at the time the treaty was negotiated, but not, I think, when the treaty was approved by parliament. In that case it was found necessary, apart from



Preservation oj Niagara Falls
the formal approval of the treaty by resolution of this parliament, to amend our legislation concerning the protection of fisheries in order to make it conform to the provisions of the treaty. We had a special statute passed at the next session, providing, for instance, penalties for violations of the treaty -because it was necessary, as my hon. friend has said, that when matters relating to the treaty were submitted to the courts there should be statutes for the purpose of enforcing its provisions. I think this course should be followed in cases where special legislation is needed. I do not think there will be need of such legislation in this case, but if there is a need there is nothing to prevent the introduction of a bill for the purpose of enforcing every provision of the treaty. I may remark that not so very long ago we were bound even by treaties which not only had not been submitted to the approval of this parliament but, still less, had not been followed by a statute of this parliament. That is changed now. We cannot be bound unless this parliament approves, and I believe that under the circumstances the method suggested by my hon. friend that in every case there should be a statute is not the method that is followed in the British parliament.

subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
It seems to me that the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has fallen into some confusion of thought in making an analysis of the legal situation as compared with the constitutional situation in Canada in respect of the ratification of treaties. I think one may suggest with great confidence that a treaty ratified by His Majesty the King in a legal sense may have full force and effect in Canada without any approval whatsoever either by resolution of this house or by statute of this parliament. Legal effect is given to many international agreements, conventions and treaties by the simple ratification by His Majesty the King. But in the constitutional sense my hon. friend has insisted that treaties, which affect and apply to Canada, prior to their ratification by His Majesty the King should receive the approval of the parliament of Canada.
]Mr. Lapointe.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me. I hope he did not misunderstand me. I never said we should do away with the approval of parliament. I am in favour of it entirely.

subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am not misrepresenting the hon. gentleman, and I think we will agree on that. But we passed a resolution in this house, two or three sessions ago, to the effect that, before the government of Canada should advise His Majesty the King to ratify any treaty or convention which in terms affected Canada, the government of Canada should first submit that treaty or convention for the approval of this parliament. Now, in this case, the government of Canada in the name of His Majesty have entered into a treaty with the United States of America, and before advising the king to ratify that treaty, the government of the day have submitted that treaty for the approval of this house. This house may give approval by simple resolution, or by a statute of parliament confirming the treaty and providing for the carrying out of its terms. What is the distinction between treaties which are approved in the one form or in the other? This convention or treaty, which is now being approved by resolution, will have no more legal effect in Canada than if it had never received the approval of this house by simple resolution. This convention which is being approved by resolution merely has that effect in Canada which it would have had at any time during the last two centuries if simply ratified by His Majesty on the advice of his privy council at Westminster.
But there may be treaties and conventions containing terms which, even if His Majesty in the exercise of his royal prerogative, ratifies them by the advice, either of his privy council in England or of his privy council in Canada, would have no legal effect whatsoever, and would not be respected or enforced by any court in this country. You have only to look through the English decisions where you will find time and again that distinguished judges of the courts have declared that treaties merely ratified by His Majesty on the advice of His Majesty's privy council in England, or by formal resolution of parliament, sometimes contain terms which are not enforceable in those courts, because they had no statutory force or effect.
Therefore, I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the clear distinction is this. Any treaty which in times past could have been ratified by His Majesty alone on the advice of his imperial privy council, and by its terms may be made applicable to all the dominions

Preservation oj Niagara Falls
and colonies without any statutory legislation by the imperial parliament or by a dominion parliament, and which could be enforced without such statutory confirmation by the imperial parliament or by the Dominion, may have full force and effect in Canada to-day if approved by a simple resolution of this house, that simple resolution being strictly a moral support to the government of the day in taking the responsibility of advising the king, through His Majesty's privy council, to effect such ratification.
If the treaty or convention, however, which is to be submitted to parliament for approval before ratification by His Majesty, affects the revenues of the country, or provides for any expenditure of public funds, then, ever since the time that Anson collected his precedents, we know that no such treaty or convention can have full force or effect until it is submitted to parliament by a bill which, previously-as in England-has been authorized by His Majesty, or until it is submitted to this parliament by a bill, which has previously been authorized by His Excellency the Governor General.
But to go further. If the treaty or convention affects property rights or interests in particular sections of this country, and the treaty is only given effect to by ratification by His Majesty on the advice of His Majesty's privy council of Canada, then no court in Canada is bound to respect such treaty which has not been confirmed by statute, except to the extent that His Majesty by the exercise of his royal prerogative could, even without the advice of his privy council in Canada, have given by his ratification such force and effect to it.
I do nbt know whether I am making my idea clear. Whether hon. gentlemen opposite accept it or not is another matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

We are not raising any
partisan discussion or issue. I called attention once before to the question as to which treaties became public law in Canada by mere ratification by His Majesty the King, and which treaties become public law in Canada only by statutory confirmation by the parliament of Canada. But take article 2 of this treaty-I am not raising objection to its terms -it provides for the construction of certain remedial works in the Niagara river above the Niagara Falls, designed to distribute the waters of the river for certain purposes. Article 2 says that concurrently with the construction and test of the remedial works, additional use of the water for hydro electric purposes may be permitted to a certain extent and subject 78594-168^
to certain conditions, and further that additional diversions shall be permitted during only a certain period of the year. Those additional diversions to be permitted in the state of New York shall not exceed a certain aggregate. Additional diversions to be permitted within the province of Ontario shall not exceed a certain daily diversion at the rate of 10,000 cubic feet per second. Now, I wish to suggest that this is one of a class of treaties .which should be confirmed by statutory enactment, because, unless it is so confirmed, any person living along the banks of the Niagara river, a riparian owner or other person interested in the flow of that water, whose rights are prejudicially affected, could go into the courts of Ontario and secure an injunction against the proposed diversion, if he showed that any right vested in him was injuriously affected thereby. And in the proceedings for injunction I suggest that this treaty dealing with private or public property interests in the province of Ontario, which has been ratified only by act of His Majesty the King and which has not been confirmed by act of this parliament, would not be considered in any court of justice as authorizing the diversion or the works which are contemplated by the terms of this treaty.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: It should be confirmed by statute?

subsubtopic: CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Yes, confirmed by statute. Therefore it seems to me we should make a clear distinction between those classes of treaties which may be ratified by His Majesty, by reason of the exercise of his royal prerogative, and by reason of the exercise of such royal prerogative be given full legal effect to in this country, and those other classes of treaties which deal with matters of public revenue and expenditure or which alienate public rights in property or which prejudicially interfere with private property rights. And the latter class, if they are to be respected and enforced by the courts of the country, should receive statutory confirmation by the parliament of Canada or by the legislature of the province. I do not wish to discuss another aspect of the question because it is dear under the constitution that certain treaties made between the empire and foreign countries may be enforced by legislation of this parliament, even although the terms of the treaty may override and conflict with legislative enactments of the provinces.

Let me say that a great deal of study has been given this matter in the past ten years by the engineers who have investigated the methods suggested by my hon. friend. Those methods have been thoroughly examined and the consensus of opinion on the part of the engineers who have advised both the provincial government and the state of New York, the federal government at Washington and our government here, was that the submerged weir would ensure the best results. The diversion of twenty thousand feet more is merely incidental to the trial of what the engineers in their judgment consider the best method whereby to preserve the scenic qualities of the falls. That is all I have to say in that respect.
As regards the question of not considering the Spray lakes matter from the same standpoint as the Niagara falls question, I may say to my hon. friend that exactly the same study was made in both cases, and that study indicated that no great damage would ensue from the proposal of the Calgary Power Company. Later on some delay occurred owing to the fact that the provincial government intervened and was desirous of utilizing this storage basin as a provincial undertaking. I must take exception to
the last statement of my colleague (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) who dismisses this weighty matter as a small affair. Hon. gentlemen in this house will feel that my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Ca'han) has rendered a very helpful service in making clear the distinction between public law and statute law, which I gather was one of his objectives in the debate.
With regard to what we are doing at the moment, I think my hon. friend will agree that we are not attempting more than to carry out the third article of the treaty, which provides that:
The present convention shall be ratified by His Britannic Majesty in accordance with constitutional practice, and by the President of the United States of America, by and with the advice and consent of the senate thereof.
As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has said, the constitutional practice which we are following in this parliament is to have all treaties approved in the first instance by both houses of parliament; and that is what just now we are seeking to have done. But it is possible that, in carrying out the provisions of the treaty, further enactments in the nature of statutes may be necessary. The only point that seems to me to come up in the -way of difference between us is whether both the approval of the treaty itself in a broad way and the statutory provisions that may be essential to the carrying out of all its provisions, must be a part of the one document and effected simultaneously.

If the Prime Minister will
pardon the interruption, I tried to make the distinction between the constitutional practice to which he is now referring, and the other

Juvenile Delinquents
practice which I shall presently mention. The constitutional practice to which the Prime Minister is now referring is a practice largely inaugurated by himself for the purpose of protecting the autonomous position of Canada, to which end he submitted to parliament his resolution that the government of Canada should not give assent to the ratification of a treaty unless approval had first been obtained from the Canadian parliament. But there is another constitutional practice of equal importance in vogue in Great Britain whereby parliament has asserted its right in respect of treaties proposed to be ratified by the king, namely: that when such treaties involve the revenues or expenditures of the country, or alienate property within the territory of the country, or prejudically affect private vested interests, in these cases it is in accord with another constitutional practice, I believe, that such treaties before ratification by His Majesty should be first approved and confirmed by imperial statute. I was trying to make that point clear.
