subtopic: CONVENTION OF 1924 BETWEEN GREAT BRITAIN AND THE UNITED STATES RESPECTING REGULATION OF LIQUOR TRAFFIC

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: CONVENTION OF 1924 BETWEEN GREAT BRITAIN AND THE UNITED STATES RESPECTING REGULATION OF LIQUOR TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the motion to go
into committee of supply to consider the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, I would ask the privilege for a few moments of referring to the enforcement of the National Prohibition Act of the United States, particularly in regard to British shipping and shipping of Canadian registry.
On January 16th, 1929, the eighteenth amendment to the constitution of the United States was ratified. That constitutional amendment inaugurated an entire change in the attitude of the government and people of the United States to the sale, transportation, exportation and importation of intoxicating 
liquors. It has one remarkable omission, that neither in the amendment itself nor in the Volstead Act, known as the National Prohibition Act, which was passed in October, 1919, is any prohibition or penalty imposed upon the purchase or consumption of intoxicating liquors within the territorial domains of the United States. Therefore those residents there who can induce others to sell may legitimately purchase, and there is no penalty imposed for their consumption of the liquor so purchased. This act came into effect in January, 1920.
To prevent the smuggling of liquor into the United States from the sea, the United States congress included in its tariff act of September, 1922, the provisions of section 581 of that act, authorizing federal officials of the United States-
-to go on board of any vessel or vehicle at any place in the United States, or within four leagues of the coast of the United States, to examine the manifest and to inspect, search and examine the vessel or vehicle, and every part thereof, and any person, trunk or package on board, and to this end hail and stop such vessel or vehicle, if under way, and to use all necessary force to compel compliance, and if it shall appear that any breach or violation of the laws of the United States has been committed whereby or in consequence of which such vessel or vehicle, or the merchandise, or any part thereof, on board of or imported by such vessel, or vehicle, is liable to forfeiture, it shall be the duty of such officer to make seizure of the same, and to arrest any person engaged in such breach or violation.
This tariff act of 1922, which has been held to foe binding upon the courts of the United States, extended their jurisdiction beyond the three-mile limit up to the twelve-mile limit, and to that extent purported to authorize infringements upon the rights of other nations beyond the three-mile limit, rights which are clearly established by the well recognized rules of international law.
Therefore, while the courts of the United States are legally bound to enforce the provisions of the tariff act of 1922, which provides for the twelve-mile limit, no other nation is bound to recognize that twelve-mile limit, and United States customs officials beyond the threenmile and up to the twelve-mile limit have, so far as established rules of international law are concerned, no right to inspect or seize vessels flying the flag of any other nation.
In discussing proposed amendments to the tariff act of 1922, Senator Sterling said that the United States Secretary, Mr. Hughes, had taken up with the British government ths question of reaching an agreement whereby searches of British vessels outside of the three-

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan
mile limit would be permitted. He stated that the Secretary of State was of the opinion:
-that the three-mile limit was generally accepted among the principal maritime nations of the world as the limit of a nation's jurisdiction over the adjacent sea, and that the government had on more than one occasion committed itself to that limit. Hence, in the view of the Secretary, there should be an international understanding or agreement in regard to the matter. Otherwise interference with foreign vessels, outside the three-mile limit, might bring about international complications and subject the government to claims for damages.
I am quoting from the Congressional Record, volume 62, Part II, page 11593. Under the conditions which then existed, the seizure by the United States coastguard service of a British vessel within twelve miles from the coast of the United States was authorized by the statute law of that country, which its courts were bound to respect but which other nations, to preserve their rights under international law, would be bound to protest. And the government of Great Britain did persistently protest against seizures of British vessels at any greater distance than three marine miles from the coast of the United States.
In 1922 the case arose of the Cunard Steamships Company versus Mellon, which is reported in 262 United States Reports, page 122. Mr. Justice Van Devanter in delivering the unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court of the United States said:
It is now settled in the United States and recognized elsewhere, that the territory subject to its jurisdiction includes the land areas under its dominion and control, the ports, harbours, bays and other enclosed arms of the sea along its coast and a marginal belt of the sea extending from the coast line outward a marine league or three geographic miles.
So that by that unanimous decision of the Supreme Court of the United States up to the three mile limit was recognized as the territorial jurisdiction of the United States, as it had been recognized throughout the British Dominions by the Territorial Waters Jurisdiction Act of 1878, which declared that:
-any part of the open sea within one marine league from the coast measured from low water mark, be deemed to be open sea within the territorial waters of Her Majesty's Dominions.
To show how completely the opinion of the Supreme Court of the United States coincided with the opinion entertained by the government of Great Britain, I find that in 1923, in 163 Commons Hansard, column 961, the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs stated the views of the British government in these terms:
The doctrine of territorial waters is not laid down in any international instrument, but the
jurisdiction of nations over coastal waters has been accepted by usage and is now a recognized rule of international law; His Majesty's government have always maintained that by international law and practice, the general limit of territorial jurisdiction is three miles, but from time to time claims to extend the three mile limit have been advanced by different states. Such claims, which amount to annexation of the high seas, could only be made effective by international agreement.
The convention between the United States and Great Britain, of 1924, had its inception in a letter written by Mr. Charles E. Hughes, United States Secretary of State, and dated June 26, 1922. This letter was addressed to the British Ambassador at Washington with regard to the possibility of aid by the British government by means of-
Cooperation on the part of the British and American authorities with regard to the smuggling of liquor.
It does seem to me most peculiar indeed that authentic copies of this correspondence between the British governments and the United States government, which was given to the press by the Department of State at Washington some two years ago and which has been cited by various legal authorities in the United States in the discussions before their own courts, and in contributions to their legal reviews, should not be available to the House of Commons of Canada, which is directly concerned in those negotiations and in the interpretation of the convention which was consummated as the result of those negotiations; because there is one rule of interpretation of treaties which I think is accepted by all modern nations, namely, that the correspondence leading up to the completion and ratification of a treaty is relevant always for the purpose of construing the purport and intent of the treaty so negotiated. Therefore it is rather surprising that when we desire to construe the terms of that convention, which has now been laid upon the table of the house, there should not be available to us the correspondence which led up to the consummation of the treaty. In this diplomatic note the United States Secretary of State, on June 26, 1922, suggested that an-
-international arrangement between the United States and Great Britain, under which the authorities of each nation would be authorized to exercise, beyond the three mile limit of territorial waters, a measure of control over vessels belonging to the other-
-was most desirable. The note proceeded to allege that:
The situation with which the authorities of this government are confronted has become so serious that this government feels prompted to inquire whether your government would be dis-

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan
posed to enter into a treaty for the purpose of checking the illegal practices in question. Such a treaty might contain reciprocal provisions authorizing the authorities of each government to exerciee the right of search of the other beyond the three mile limit of territorial waters, to the extent of twelve miles from the shore.
There was implied in that note an admission that the United States government had a right of search and seizure within the territorial limit of three miles, but that its right of search and seizure between the limit of three miles and the limit of twelve miles, enacted by the United States Tariff Act of 1922, depended upon the acquiescence of foreign governments.
On November 13, 1922, the British government replied at length, stating in detail the measures which they had taken to prevent breaches of British laws by persons engaged in the liquor trade with the United States. The British note then proceeds:
His Majesty's government had thus taken steps, even before the receipt of representations from the United States government, to prevent the practices, to which attention has now been drawn. They have now, as already indicated, issued supplementary instructions in the matter and hope that the measures taken will prove successful in preventing any breaches of the local law. They feel, however, more difficulty in accepting the proposal that a treaty should be made authorizing the authorities of each government to exercise a right of search of vessels of the other beyond the three mile limit of territorial waters up to a distance of twelve miles from the shore.	.
His Majesty's government have consistently opposed any extension of the limit of territorial waters such as that now suggested. They feel that the outbreak of smuggling which has led to the proposal cannot be regarded as a permanent condition, but is one which will no doubt be suppressed by the United States authorities within the not-distant future. While, therefore, they are desirous of assisting the United States government to the best of their ability in the suppression of the traffic and in the prevention of the abuse of the British flag by those engaged in it, they do not feel that they can properly acquiesce, in order to meet a temporary emergency, in the abandonment of a principle to which they attach great importance.
In communicating the above to you I am directed to add that while His Majesty's government are, as already indicated, unable to acquiesce in the proposed treaty for the extension of territorial waters, they are nevertheless most desirous of taking any steps within their power to prevent any infractions of the local law by persons engaged in liquor smuggling.
In the meantime, on September 13, 1922, the British vessel Gardner was seized twenty-two miles from the coast of the United States, and the British government protested against this seizure on the ground that it had taken place beyond the three mile limit. On account

of, or at least following, this protest by the British government, on November 9, 1922, instructions were issued to the United States collector of customs by the United States Secretary of the Treasury, as follows:
The department is in receipt of your telegram of the 8th instant, relative to the seizure of the British auxiliary schooner M. M. Gardner on September 13, 1922.
It appears from your report that the seizure was made outside the three mile limit, and that while the master admitted unloading part of the cargo beyond the three mile limit there is no evidence that the vessel was communicating with the shore by means of her own small boats or equipment. Under these circumstances it is the desire of the Department of State and the Department of Justice that all foreign vessels so seized shall be released, and you will be governed accordingly. A report should be made to the department in each instance.
So that the government of the United States at that time, even before the negotiation of the treaty, by its acts and its orders, acquiesced in the contentions contained in the protest of the British government. The newspapers at that time reported that approximately twenty vessels were released under this order, but the United States government retained possession of a British vessel named the Grace' and Ruby, which they claimed had been searched and seized beyond the three mile limit but which had been in communication with the shore by means of her small boats. In regard to the retention of the Grace and Ruby, on December 30, 1922, the British ambassador wrote the United States Department of State as follows:
In order to avoid the possibility of any misunderstanding, I am desired by my government to make it clear that His Majesty's government are unable to acquiesce in what they understand to be the ruling of the United States government, namely, that foreign vessels may be seized outside the three mile limit if it can be shown that they have established contact with the shore for illegal purposes by means of their own small boats. My government must reserve their right to lodge a protest in any individual case in which action may be taken by the United States government under this ruling.
That was a clear protest on the part of the British government against the search and seizure beyond the three-mile limit of British vessels which were or had been in communication by their own boats with the coast of the United States.
On January 18, 1923, the United States Secretary of State replied as follows:
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your note, No. 973, of December 30, 1922, stating that your government desires you to make it clear that it is unable to acquiesce in what it understands to be the ruling of the United States government, namely, that foreign vessels may be seized outside the three-mile limit if it can be shown that they have estab-

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan
lished contact with the shore for illegal purposes by means of their own small boats. You state that your government must reserve the right to lodge a protest in any individual case in which action may be taken by the United States government in cases of this character.
I have the honour to state that consideration has been given to the statements contained in your note, and the conclusion has been reached that the government of the United States should adhere to the position it has previously taken, that foreign vessels outside the three-mile limit may be seized when it is established that they are using their email boats in illegal operations within the three-mile limit of the United States. This conclusion is supported by the position taken by the British government in the oase of the British Columbia schooner Araunah, which was seized off Copper island, by the Russian authorities in 1888, because it appeared that members of the crew of the schooner were illegally taking seals in Behring sea by means of canoes operated between the schooner and the land, and it was affirmed that two of the canoes were within half a mile of the shore. Lord Salisbury stated that Her Majesty's government were of opinion that, even if the Araunah at the time of the seizure was herself outside the three-mile territorial limit, the fact that she was, iby means of her boats, carrying on fishing within Russian waters without the prescribed license warranted her seizure and confiscation according to the provisions of the municipal law regulating the use of those waters.
Therefore the negotiations at that period had this result: The United States abandoned their claim that they had the right to seize British vessels outside the three-mile limit except those which were communicating for illegal purposes, or in breach of the laws of the United States, with the shore of that country by their own boats. On April 30, 1923, that was followed by a statement made by Mr. McNeill, Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, in the British House of Commons at Westminster, in which, referring to the case of the Grace and Ruby, he said:
His Majesty's government have questioned the right of the United States government to make this seizure, and diplomatic correspondence on the subject is proceeding.
Therefore, at that time the government of Great Britain did not acquiesce even in the claim of the United States government that it had a right to seize beyond the three-mile limit British vessels which were in communication with the shore by their own small boats.
On July 10, 1923, the British Charge d'Affaires at Washington wrote to the United States Secretary of State in reference to the condemnation of the Henry L. Marshall, which was alleged to have transferred her cargo of liquor to an American vessel at a point ten miles off the coast of the United States; he stated that this vessel was not entitled to British registry. There had been
a fraudulent transfer to British registry, the vessel really being owned by a citizen of the United States, and the British government intimated that they did not intend to exercise their diplomatic privileges for the protection of an American who had procured a fraudulent certificate of registry under British law. However, the British Charge d'Affaires continued:
In order to avoid the possibility of any misunderstanding on the part of the United States government as to His Majesty's government's attitude in this matter I have the honour, under instructions from His Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, to inform you that any attempt on the part of the United States authorities to seize a British ship outside the three-mile limit would be regarded by His Majesty's government as creating a very serious situation. In regard to the Henry L. Marshall case, I have been instructed to explain that the absence of a protest by His Majesty's government against the condemnation of this vessel in no way implies any alteration lin the views of His Majesty's government with regard to the principle at stake, inasmuch, as that vessel, owing to the circumstances in which she secured her British registry, was not recognized by His Majesty's government as entitled to British registry. Consequently. His Majesty's government have not felt called upon to assert the principle at stake on her behalf, since, as far as His Majesty's government are concerned, the Henry L. Marshall remains an American vessel.
Again, in diplomatic language, the British government made a most emphatic protest against the seizure of this vessel beyond the three-mile limit from the American coast. On July 16, 1923, before the negotiations for the 1924 liquor convention were consummated, Mr. Charles E. Hughes, United States Secretary of State, replied to the note which I have just read, justifying the seizure of a British vessel if the facts show-I quote:
__that its direct and single effort was by
fraudulent means to introduce the cargo, and all of it within the territory of the United States; and that the vessel prior to and at the time of its actual seizure, even though more than three miles from the shore, was hovering off the coasts of the United States and engaged in an attempt to violate the laws of the_United States by the introduction of liquor into its territory.
This is the first time that the American doctrine was expressed that vessels hovering near the three-mile limit, but just beyond that limit, were liable to seizure by the United States authorities and thereupon liable to forfeiture by decree of the United States federal courts.
In the meantime a draft treaty had been prepared by Mr. Hughes, Secretary of State, and submitted on behalf of the government of the United States to the British Secretary
Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan

of State for Foreign Affairs. The terms of the draft treaty proposed that each of the two governments would be permitted to board vessels of the other within a distance of twelve geographical miles from the coast, in order to make inquiry whether such vessels or the persons on board were engaged in an attempt to violate the laws of the other party to the proposed treaty. That was a clear suggestion of the desire of the United States to incorporate into the rules of international law, which limited the territorial jurisdiction to three miles, that provision of the United States Tariff Act of 1922 which extended the jurisdiction of their officials and of their courts to a limit of twelve miles from their coasts. In pursuing the discussion on this treaty, on July 19, 1923, Mr. Hughes, the Secretary of States for the United States, wrote to the British government making an official declaration. Before I read that declaration I wish again to emphasize the contention that in respect of a treaty which intimately concerns the Dominion of Canada, and in the interpretation of which the correspondence which preceded its ratification is absolutely necessary for a clear understanding of its import, we should not be denied access to that official correspondence. I have a part of that correspondence as published in the American press and also as quoted in some of the briefs submitted rto the United States federal courts in cases arising out of the seizure of British vessels. Mr. Hughes made this declaration:
The proposed special agreement would bear only upon those vessels which came within twelve miles but hover off the three-mile limit for the purpose of aiding in the smuggling of intoxicating liquor, or other prohibited articles, into the territory of the United States.
That is a clear declaration that the proposed special agreement would give the United States government officials the right of search and seizure only within the proposed twelve-mile limit of the original draft agreement. Mr. Hughes proceeds:
It may confidently be asserted that there would be no disposition on the part of the American authorities, and' the special agreement would not justify any attempt, to seize a British vessel, save within the limits proposed and when it was clear that the vessel concerned was directly involved in an attempt to introduce its illicit cargo into the territory of the United States.
I think that declaration is one which binds the honour of the government of the United States in dealing with these seizures of British and Canadian vessels beyond the three-mile limit; it was a declaration involving the honour of the United States that no seizures

would be made beyond the limit provided for in the draft agreement which was subsequently consummated, signed, ratified and confirmed by this parliament of Canada-
On September 17, 1923, the British government replied, saying:
So far as British subjects are concerned, there is no violation of any law, British or international, in the sale of such liquors on the high seas to purchasers of any nationality; therefore there is no obligation upon His Majesty's government to interfere with the prosecution of a perfectly legitimate trade. Nevertheless, the whole question has been carefully examined with an earnest desire to afford the United States government any proper assistance in the difficulties which they are encountering in the enforcement of the Volstead Act.
I then omit some matter which is irrelevant for my purpose, and the note concludes:
I am to add, in view of the difficulties of the ease, that His Majesty's government could not agree to the extension of the three-mile limit, even for a limited purpose, until the matter has been submitted to the imperial conference. which will meet within a few weeks in London.
These negotiations clearly disclosed that the British government objected to fixing a distance defined in miles for the exercise of the proposed search and seizure beyond the fixed territorial limit of three miles from the shore; but that, if the territorial limit of three miles were affirmed, the British government was willing to agree not to object to the boarding and search of vessels flying the British flag "outside the limit of territorial waters," but not at a greater distance from the coast than can be "traversed in one hour" by the vessel suspected of committing the offence, except in those cases where the cargo of liquor is intended to be conveyed to the shore by a vessel other than the one boarded and searched, in which event the distance from the shore is determined by the speed of the other vessel.
While these negotiations were pending and under discussion by the two governments, a meeting of the American Society of International Law, held at Washington, D.C., in April, 1923, discussed the matters then at issue in the correspondence between the government of the United States and the government of Great Britain. Mr. Frederick K. Nielson, counsel with the United States Department of State, was present at that conference. His remarks I have taken from the proceedings of the American Society of International Law for the year 1923, at page 38. After Mr. Nielson had stated the position

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan
which the United States government had taken in years past with respect to the freedom of the seas beyond the three-mile limit, he said:
I have tried to emphasize the position taken by the United States in the past. It seems clear that until an appropriate agreement respecting the alteration of the well-established rule shall have been reached, the United States, in view particularly of this positive position, cannot justify a departure from that rule for the purpose of dealing with an isolated or temporary situation.
He was referring to the isolated or temporary situation which was created by the enforcement of the Volstead Act and the eighteenth amendment throughout United States territory. At page 46 of the report, Mr. Nielson continued:
Writers who have discussed the so-called Hovering Acts, authorizing the boarding of vessels on the high seas bound for a port, point out that such action cannot be taken pursuant to the exercise of a right, but that it is a permissive jurisdiction in which a nation whose vessels are boarded may acquiesce.
I should like to call the attention of the Prime Minister to that remark, which I believe to be a correct statement of a rule of international law. Mr. Nielson continued:
Of course the action authorized by the so-called Hovering Acts is something different from undertaking to interfere generally with vessels beyond the three mile limit with a view to the prevention of smuggling. We can hardly expect nations to acquiesce generally in such action solely for the purpose of preventing smuggling. The violation of our law is, to be sure, a serious thing, but to other nations there is merely presented a ease of difficulty in preventing smuggling. They do not think that drinking wine will destroy or degrade their civilizations. I do not know whether it will or not. I have never made any sociological studies along those lines, but as I say, they do not consider the question so serious as to warrant its being dealt with pursuant to principles underlying the so-called right of selfpreservation, and surely they would never concur in the idea expressed by Doctor Stowell-
Who had preceded him.
-as I understood him, that they would assist us in punishing infractions of our laws relating to smuggling. We have enacted such laws and it is incumbent upon us to enforce them. They, of course, concede our sovereign right to do so within our jurisdiction. Surely, they will not admit our right to call upon them to help us exercise our sovereign rights. And in view of positive statements often heard in this country with regard to exclusive sovereign rights, to deal with matters relating to control overimports and immigration, it might not be considered desirable by the people of the United States that foreign countries should volunteer to help us to enforce those rights.

speechtext:
Those of the counsel with the United 'States State department, Mr. Nielson. At this stage-in November, 1923-the imperial conference assembled at London, and in the correspondence and documents recently brought down by the Prime Minister I find this extract from the summary of the imperial conference of 1923:
* During the session of the conference, the question of the regulation of the liquor traffic off the American coasts and of the measures to be taken to avoid a serious conflict either of public opinion or of official action was seriously debated. The conference arrived at the conclusion that while affirming and safeguarding as a cardinal feature of British policy the principle of the three-mile limit, it was yet both desirable and practicable to meet the American request for an extension of the right of search beyond this limit for the above purpose, and negotiations were at once opened with the United States government for the conclusion of an experimental agreement with this object in view.
There was a clear statement of the understanding of the representatives of the various dominions and the British government at that imperial conference in 1923, namely, that, assuming, as they did assume, and as they had a right to assume, that the United States had no right of search beyond the three-mile limit from her coast, nevertheless, in order to assist the United States in the enforcement of its smuggling and other tariff laws it was expedient to meet the United States request for an extension of the right of search beyond this limit for the above purpose, and negotiations were undertaken with that end in view.
I should like to place the treaty on Hansard where it can be read by everyone who takes Hansard, but I suppose I shall not be permitted to do that and I do not wish to take up the time of the house in doing so. Is there any objection?

speechtext:
That treaty should 'be known throughout the length and breadth of this country. It is as follows:

And the President of the United States of America;

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan

treaties had authorized the proceedings avowed in the record before the court. He also added:
Nowhere in the treaty can any words be found indicating .an intent on the part of the contracting parties to change or extend the limits of the territory of the United States. In fact, the contrary is plainly indicated by Article 1 of each treaty.
Then there arose the case which was heard in 1926 of the Francis E., a British vessel, seized sixteen miles off the Florida coast. On appeal in that case, the circuit court of appeals for the district, a federal court, held:
There is nothing in the treaty from which it could reasonably be inferred that it was the intention of the high contracting parties to extend the criminal laws of the United States beyond the three-mile limit. The vessel may be seized if those on hoard have violated any law within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States that would subject her to forfeiture except as to provisions relative to sea-stores and compensation for loss occasioned by improper acts, not germane to the subject here under discussion. That is the extent of the agreement.
Referring to the treaty, the court also held that "the American-Rritish treaty did not in fact enact criminal legislation" and that no statute had yet Ibeen enacted by the United States making illegal the acts committed1 by foreigners on foreign ships on the high seas, nineteen miles from the coast of the United States.
After I had run these cases down, through the courtesy of the Department of External Affairs, I had access to Jessup, an American authority, who has recently issued a work dealing with marginal waters. After referring to these cases to Which I have called attention, Jessup says that the weight of judicial authority-
-certainly sustains the view first enunciated by Judge Morton, in the case of the Frances Louise, that ithe treaties deal completely with the subject and exclude all extraterritorial seizures not made in conformity with its terms.
I have some other cases, but I do not wish to tax the patience of the house.
I wish to direct the attention of hon. members to the correspondence which has been laid on the table by the Prime Minister between the Hon. Vincent Massey, Canada's representative at Washington, and the State Department of the United States relating to the sinking of the Canadian vessel I'm Alone. The first letter is of March 28, 1929, addressed by Mr. W. R. Castle, Jr., for the United States Secretary of State, to the Hon. Vincent Massey, and simply recounts the facts from the American report. The reply is dated April 9, 1929, and is subscribed by the Hon. Vincent Massey, and directed to the Hon. Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State of the

United States. The Canadian government takes a very, very strong position, a position I think irrefutable in law, in view of the terms of the convention of 1924 and of the correspondence which I have cited to-night and the decisions of the American courts to which I have made allusion. Paragraph 8 says:
It was of the essence of the convention that its provisions covered the whole field of extraterritorial seizures.
So far as I am concerned, I am not disposed to be critical, but I wish, for the sake of preserving a strong position on the part of the Canadian government for all future time, that that note had practically endedl with paragraph 8. I am sure the government will agree with this proposition, that, in our diplomatic correspondence with foreign governments, any formal admission made by this government stands registered for all time against any future claims of this country arising out of a similar situation; and therefore it is very necessary indeed that statements of law should be made only after the most careful consideration and reflection, and that they should be made in such express terms as to leave no doubt whatsoever as to their meaning. This note of Mr. Massey is in the nature of a pleading before a court. I do not know who wrote it, but I am sure that, if he had been accustomed to preparing pleadings in our courts of law, he would realize the advisability on all occasions of stating one's client's case quite fully both as to the facts and the law on, which he based his claim; but it is always advantageous to leave the opposing attorney to state his own case, so that in reply you may place your own objections more pertinently and expressly before the court which is to consider the issues. In paragraph 12 of this letter Mr. Massey continues:
In any ease the pursuit lasted through two days and two nights, f'ar beyond the starting point, and the sinking took place over two hundred miles southward in open sea. It has been intimated that pursuit and seizure on the high seas might be justified on the ground of hot and continuous pursuit. It is agreed that international law recognizes that pursuit begun within territorial waters may be continued on the high seas, if immediate and continuous.
Now, first, in the prior correspondence there was no such intimation as Mr. Massey suggests. It had not been intimated that pursuit and seizure on the high seas might be justified on the ground of hot and continuous pursuit. It might better have been left to the American Secretary of State to make that contention, and, in my opinion, such an ad-

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan
mission should not in any event have been made on behalf of this government. It will be noted that Mr. Massey proceeds:
It is agreed that international law recognizes that pursuit begun within territorial waiters may be continued on the high seas, if immediate and continuous.
I take this opportunity of suggesting that that is not a statement of international law which is generally recognized to-day, and that the admission so made may prove most prejudicial to the interests of Canada in this prospective arbitration, and possibly most prejudicial to the interests of Canada in such cases as may subsequently arise during the existence of that treaty. After making that admission Mr. Massey proceeds:
The validity of this doctrine has been fully recognized by the Canadian courts.
I beg to suggest that there is only one case in which this doctrine has come before the Canadian courts, and I also suggest that it has not been recognized to the extent and in the terms which Mr. Massey has expressed. I refer to the case of the ship North versus the King, reported in the Supreme Court of Canada reports, .volume 47, page 385, et sequitur. I wish to call attention to the decision of Mr. Justice Davies,-more recently known, before he died, as Sir Louis Davies,- who gave the decision of the majority of the court. But first let me state the facts under which the decision arose.
The American schooner North was discovered fishing illegally within the three-mile limit with four of her boats out fishing within three miles of the Pacific coast in violation of the treaty of 1818. One of these boats was seized by the Canadian fisheries protection cruiser "Ke'strel". The North was pursued and overhauled one and three-quarters miles beyond the three-mile limit. Her boats were out within the three-mile limit, and the "Kestrel" was delayed in overtaking her by stopping to seize one of these boats. Now the North was seized, it is true, beyond the three-mile limit. It was a hot and continuous pursuit. But if I understand that decision correctly, our Supreme Court held that, in the case as between the owners of the American vessel and the King, they were not called upon to consider or to decide whether the vessel had been rightfully seized in accordance with the rules of international law, at the point where she was seized, one and three-quarters miles beyond the three-mile limit. The court held that although the seizure may have been illegal and the first arrest illegal, inasmuch as the vessel was brought within the jurisdiction of Canada, and a proper attachment made 78594-1691
subsequently to her being brought into Canadian waters, the court could decide on forfeiture as against the owners, leaving the government of the United States-the vessel being of American registry-either to acquiesce in the seizure having been made, at the place where it was made, or to make a claim for damages on behalf of the owners, which claim would be settled 'by some international tribunal. Mr. Justice Davies said:
But even if there was a reasonable doubt as to the power of the officers of the cruiser to seize the schooner on the high seas beyond the three-mile limit, under the circumstances before us, I am of the opinion that such irregularity could not affect the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court to hear and determine the offence charged against the schooner. That offence being within the jurisdiction of the court and the vessel being also within such jurisdiction and properly attached and libelled could not plead an alleged irregularity in the mode of her being taken on the high seas as a defence.
The manner in which she was brought into port and within the jurisdiction of the court was. if wrong or irregular, matter for diplomatic protest at the instance of the country to which she belonged or for civil action by the owners of the ship. If that country does not complain of any offence against its honour and dignity the ship libelled cannot do so. If the poaching schooner had escaped into the territorial waters of her own country and had been chased there, captured and brought back the government of that country might well justify intervention. But short of such intervention I think the ship charged with illegal fishing within the three-mile limit being within the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court and properly libelled there for an offence committed within its jurisdiction procedings cannot be defeated or the jurisdiction of the court ousted merely by an irregularity in the taking of the ship.
The principle underlying the decisions relating to persons kidnapped and brought before magistrates having jurisdiction over the offence with which they are charged are, I think, in point. These cases show that the remedy for the illegal arrest and the kidnapping of the prisoner is by proceedings at the instance of the government of the foreign country whose law or territory has been violated or at the suit of the injured party against the trespasser.
This doctrine of hot pursuit has been suggested at times by the United States in respect of the pursuit of vessels which have been found within the three-mile limit, committing offences against the customs laws of the United States and which, when an attempt has been made to seize them, have escaped beyond the three-mile limit and have been seized. But I suggest that no British authority has ever made the clear, bald admission, with respect to the validity of this American doctrine of hot pursuit, in the terms in which Mr. Massey makes it in the note from which I have just quoted. And although up to this time the Americans had never suggested in this correspondence that
Liquor Traffic-Mr. Cahan

they could vindicate their actions by reason of the hot pursuit of the I'm Alone, Mr. Massey continues in paragraph 14:
It is believed, however, that the government of United States will agree that it is essential for the effective operation of the convention of January, 1924, and for the attainment of the definite and agreed procedure, which was the object of the contracting parties, that the terms of the convention should be strictly observed.
Having thus taken his ground accurately, in express terms and in the most convincing manner, he nevertheless proceeds in the next sentence:
His Majesty's government in Canada trusts that the government of the United States will further agree that the search and seizure of vessels beyond territorial waters should be exercised in accordance *with the terms of the convention,-
Splendid; but he unfortunately adds:
-that pursuit should not be continued beyond an hour's sailing distance from the shore unless initiated within territorial waters.
This subsidiary contention destroys the force and effect of his main and valid argument that the United States had no jurisdiction beyond such limits os are defined within the four corners of the treaty. He says that pursuit should not be continued beyond an hour's sailing distance from the shore unless initiated within territorial waters; but dearly the whole purpose and intent of the convention was that pursuit, hot or otherwise, wherever initiated, could never be carried beyond the distance covered by one hour's sail of the pursued vessel from the coast of the United States. To determine that fact, and to secure from the United States an agreement to that end, was the sole. purpose of the long continued negotiations between Great Britain and the United States. Moreover, it was due to the express declaration of the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Hughes, to which declaration I have ilready referred, that under this convention there would be no seizure beyond the twelve-mile limit, that the government of Great Britain and, I believe, the government of Canada also were induced to approve of and authorize the ratification of that treaty. That the United States Secretary of State very speedily placed his finger on the weak point in our contention will appear from his letter of April 17, 1929. It is to be found on page 15 of this printed report, about two thirds of the distance down the' page:
It is not understood that your government questions the validity of the doctrine of hot pursuit as such but merely its application in the instant case.

Then he goes on to suggest that since Mr. Massey has attached the doctrine of hot pursuit to the express terms of the convention of 1924 he, on behalf of the United States, will press his new vantage point to the extreme. He says:
In the estimation of this government, the correct principle underlying the doctrine of hot pursuit is that if the arrest would have been valid when the vessel was first hailed, but was made impossible through the illegal action of the pursued vessel in failing to stop when ordered to do so, then hot pursuit is justified and the locus of the arrest and the distance of the pursuit are immaterial, provided:
(1)	That it was without the territorial waters of any other state;
(2)	That the pursuit has been hot and continuous.
Then I would direct attention to the final letter from Mr. Massey, the date of which does not appear to be printed. Paragraph 5 of that letter reads as follows:
5. Even, however, were it not established that the I'm Alone was beyond the treaty limits when ordered to stop, the government of Canada cannot agree that any adequate ground has been established for pursuit on the high seas. They have previously indicated their view that the doctrine of hot pursuit which has been advanced is not applicable to a pursuit which, as is agreed to have been the case in the present instance, did not begin in territorial waters.
There we are endeavouring to limit the application of the doctrine of hot pursuit which we, quite unnecessarily, were led or induced to admit in the very first statement which we made as to our legal position.
I simply wish to direct attention to this and to suggest that if we are to engage in diplomatic correspondence of this nature with other countries, dealing with the rights of Canadian citizens on the high seas or in other parts of the world, it is absolutely necessary that our Department of External Affairs should obtain access to the Department of Justice for legal advice; if that access is not open at the present time, or, if that department is not now thoroughly equipped to deal with the international issues which are sure to arise from time to time, immediate steps should be taken to provide for such thoroughly experienced and competent legal advice as is certainly necessary in dealing with a nation such as the United States which, I say with deliberation, having, through the United States Secretary of State, pledged its honour to one interpretation of that treaty in the most formal manner, now undertakes to sink British shipping on the high seas and to bolster its act of almost deliberate wanitonnees, by developing an entirely different interpretation

Liquor Traffic-Mr. Mackenzie King
of an international convention, which, in its plain terms, does not admit of any such construction.
It seems very clear to me-and I say this deliberately-that under the tariff laws of the United States as they may be construed by their express terms, the coastguard of the United States was not authorized to seize British or any other shipping, save perhaps American shipping, at any point more than twelve miles distant from its coast. In this case the evidence seems clear that this pursuit of two days continued to a point on the high seas 215 miles from the coast, and in my opinion the second coastguard vessel, the Dexter I think, which then came upon the scene, would never have sunk a British ship by cannon shot 215 miles from the coast, unless by wireless she had received direct instructions from the political authorities of the United States to commit that act which, if actually authorized by the executive political authority of that country, was an act of war, or which, if not authorized by that political authority but actually committed on the initiative of the United) States coastguard alone, was the equivalent of an act of deliberate piracy.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the
house will recognize that in discussing a matter which has been referred to arbitration under an important treaty the government occupies a position very different from that occupied by an hon. member of this house who also happens to be a member of the opposition. Certainly it would be an extraordinary procedure were the government, in the circumstances, to argue with my hon. friend with respect to any aspect of the case.
As a result of correspondence which has taken plaee between the two governments the I'm Alone incident has been referred to arbitration, and the arbitrators are about to be appointed. In these circumstances I think any criticism 'which the opposition may have to take against the administration, considering all the factors, might well be raised at a time when it is not calculated to embarrass
in any particular those who will be charged with presenting the Canadian side of the case.
May I say that with respect to the correspondence which Mr. Massey, as the Canadian minister at Washington, presented to the American government, our government of course takes full responsibility. Mr. Massey acted under the instructions of the government, and any criticism which may be directed against aniy communication of his would be properly directed against the administration itself.
My hon. friend has spoken at great length and has given a very lucid and comprehensive statement of the grounds on which he believes the case should be decided in favour of Canada. In so doing he has displayed his great abilities as a counsel, but again I submit that in the interests of the country at large he might have presented his argument to better effect in some other form to those who are at present at work upon this case.
I shall not attempt in any way to review .what my hon. friend has said. He began by speaking of the 'domestic law of the United States of 1922 with respect to the tariff and certain discussions which related thereto. He then reviewed at some length the cases of seizures which had taken place beyond the three-mile limit prior to the enactment of the convention to which he subsequently referred. He made mention of a remark by the Hon. Mr. Hughes, Secretary of State of the United States, which he said in honour bound the United States to a certain position, and having said that much he then came to the convention under which the I'm Alone incident has arisen and said that everything relevant to that particular incident must be contained within the four corners of the convention; in other words, all that he had said up to that time was more or less beside the mark.

speechtext: It is being submitted to arbitration and a thorough ironing out by the arbitrators will be made. I represent the owners of the cargo and the schooner, and as such I want to say that we are thoroughly satisfied with the present status of the case. There is only one observation I have to make with respect to that at the present time, because the whole matter will be under consideration before we finish the estimates. But, there must be some principle governing matters of this kind. In some instances the increase in the salaries of the deputy heads has been $1,000 and in others $2,000, while still other deputy heads have received no increase at all. Perhaps the Prime Minister as the head of the administration would give us some idea on what basis these increases have been granted. speechtext:
I think my

There are some branches of the government service which have at their head officers with the rank of deputy, but who are not deputy ministers in the sense in which the word is used without qualification. The question of their increase has not been finally considered up to the present time. There are important officers of state performing duties, some of them undoubtedly of a character similar to those performed by a deputy head. As I have said, up to the present time their position has not been finally considered by the government. We felt that inasmuch as a commission was being appointed to inquire into the whole question of the salaries of those who are expected to have technical and professional qualifications, its members would wish to consider the cases of all those in the public service who hold positions which demand qualifications of that kind. Later the government may have something to say with regard to the additional remuneration, if any, to be accorded to them. But certainly with the difficulty the government is experiencing in retaining the services of some of those who are at the head of the departments of state, it has been felt that, having regard to the salaries paid for similar services by private organizations, and having regard also to the length and quality of the services rendered, we should make the increases which we have made.

I think, Mr. Chairman,
the observations of the Prime Minister answered a portion of the questions which I asked. The maximum appears to be $10,000. Now, if there has been an increase in the amount of work that has to be done by deputy ministers, I should think in one department in which it would be reflected, if not two, there has been no increase, apparently $10,000 being the maximum. Then there are other departments which are being gradually shorn of their responsibilities, by reason of the provinces being likely to receive their resources some time in the next century, and presumably those deputies having less work

With respect to others we have increases of $1,000 and $2,000, and, as I have said, neither upon the basis of length of service and character of the work rendered, nor upon any other factor of that character, could you say why one should receive an increase of $1,000 and another $2,000. It is a little difficult to reconcile these various factors in order to arrive at a common policy. It has been suggested that the political predilections of some of the gentlemen before they were appointed have had a great deal to do with determining whether or not they should receive additional compensation. That has been stated by friends in and out of the house who have not been considered. It is a matter, I think, upon which a statement should be .made.
I do agree with the Prime Minister that it is difficult nowadays to get men to remain in government service. There has never been a time when the demand for competent and qualified executives was greater than it is to-day, and if the country is to be well served it must be prepared to pay. The difficulty I experience in connection with the whole matter is that we have a multiplication of employees in Canada to whom we pay indifferent wages and compensation, with the result of a steady increase of the number, spreading over too wide an area-spreading it very thinly, if I may use a term that is easily understood-the number which would give efficient service. I listened to some explanations made during the passing of the estimates the other night, and as I thought over what was involved I began to understand why the minister was unable to recommend any increase having regard to the number employed. Friends of mine who have been in London have made a very striking comparison between the High Commissioner from Canada and the High Commissioner from Australia in relation to the duties performed by these gentlemen, and I regret to say that the comparison is not to the credit of this country. Most visitors seem to think that the Canadian High Commissioner is there more or less for the purpose of introducing Canadians to high society, and I think it would be well for the Prime Minister, if it is possible for him to do so, to dispel such an idea and give the committee an understanding of the High Commissioner's duties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No one
familiar with the important and varied duties of the High Commissioner could entertain such an idea. The Canadian High Commissioner represents the government of Canada in innumerable transactions, and particularly in its relation with the government of Great Britain. For the barest outline of last year's activities I would refer my hon. friend to page 10 of the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. At the bottom of the page he will find an account of a few of the duties performed by the office of the High Commissioner during 1928. Perhaps I might read a paragraph in point:
The High Commissioner's office in London has discharged its usual multifarious and important duties, acting as the organ for maintaining the necessary detailed relations between the departments of His Majesty's governments in Canada and Great Britain, as well as in connection with the government expenditures and contracts in Great Britain, with measures foT informing the British public as to Canadian matters and extending requisite assistance to Canadian visitors. The office was represented at the periodical meetings of the Pacific Cable Board, the Imperial Institute, the War Graves Commission, and the Imperial Shipping Committee.
In pursuance of his usual practice with the object of keeping in close touch with Canadian public life, the High Commissioner visited the Dominion during the month of August, delivering speeches and holding interviews at various places. He was actively engaged also in the conclusion of an agreement with the Bulgarian government under which the property of Bulgarian nationals in Canada sequestrated by the Custodian of Enemy Property is to be restored to them, 'and also in the arrangements connected with the transfer to the Royal Canadian Navy of the Champlain and Vancouver as well as the building of two new destroyers for the Canadian navy.
Supply-External Affairs

This makes no mention of the many financial transactions for which the High Com-misioner's office has been responsible in part in the past and is responsible at the present time-for example the collecting of outstanding debts from the governments of Great Britain, Roumania and Greece, as well as many other highly important transactions. It may be stated that the High Commissioner in cooperation with the Minister of Finance was instrumental in securing, during the seven years Mr. Larkin has been in office, the settlement of outstanding accounts resulting from war transactions, averaging $29,500,000 per annum. As one instance of the effective service of the High Commissioner during the past year I would mention his success in cooperation with the Imperial Shipping Committee in doing away with the discriminations previously in force in the insurance rates charged by the underwriters upon ships voyaging to Canadian ports, particularly Halifax and St. John and in some measure St. Lawrence and British Columbia ports, a practical service to every Canadian exporter and importer.
I do not know from what source my hon. friend Obtained the information which occasioned him to make the comparison he did between the High Commissioner for Australia and the High Commissioner for Canada. Nothing could possibly be further from the mark. I think anyone who has any knowledge of the work being done in London by Canada's High Commissioner will say that we have been extremely fortunate in having in the Honourable Mr. Larkin a gentleman of exceptional business ability and administrative capacity and one who has been most industrious and efficient in watching over Canada's interests in London. I think Canada's office will more than bear comparison with any similar office in Great Britain.

In support of the criticism of the hon. member for Acadia I may say that I visited London in 1927, and from my inspection of Canada House as compared, say, with Australia House, I would say that we do not go far enough in advertising Canada except possibly in the advertising matter which is on the shelves of the ground floor. It is a very nice office and they have very fine reception rooms, but when it comes to the advertising the wares of Canada certainly we can take a leaf from Australia's book; from a commercial point of view there is no comparison between the two. If you go into Australia House-and any members who have been there will support me in this statement- 
you will find a miniature Australia before you; you will see every state; you will see pictures of the various industries, of the fields and of the farms; their products are on display where any vistor can see them. On the other hand, if you go to Canada House you will find a very nice office, and commodious waiting and reception rooms, but that is all you can say. What the high commissioner does there in his capacity as Canada's representative I cannot say. The Prime Minister is in a position to give the house that information, but from the point of view of advertising Canada to the public I certainly think we take second place to Australia.

I should like to say a few words with regard to the statement made by the hon. member for Battle River. He forgets that Australia concentrates entirely on London; all the advertising they do in Great Britain with regard to the products of Australia is done in the city of London, and as far as London is concerned it is well done. However, my hon. friend must bear in mind that Canada has ten offices in the principal cities of Great Britain, where splendid exhibitions of Canadian products are maintained, advertising Canada all over Great Britain. We consider that a much better way of advertising Canada than by concentrating everything in London where it can be seen only by the .people of that city

Would the Prime Minister tell us, without going into great detail, the reason for the $5,000 increase, excluding the $2,000 increase in the salary of the High Commissioner?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Due to the increased work of the London office-and I may say this work has grown considerably even within the last year coincident with our having in Canada a High Commissioner from Great Britain-we have thought it advisable to make provision for another clerk in the Canada House office, and there is an appropriation of $3,000 for that purpose.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister if this $2,000 increase was requested or suggested by the High Commissioner, or whether it is a bonus offered by the right hon. gentleman himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that it was not asked by the High Commissioner. As I said a moment ago, the department is seeking to adopt some uniformity in the scale of allowances for salaries and other purposes as between the different offices. AVe have felt that London is the first of the positions abroad, and that the salaries and allowances should be made proportionate in relation to what is being paid elsewhere. I do not think I am wrong in saying that the High Commissioner spends many times the total of his salary and allowance in connection with the services which he is rendering the country overseas.
He must spend at least

speechtext:
I am sure it is more than that.

I think the Prime Minister is absolutely right when he says that the High Commissioner spends more money than he is paid by this government. What I am afraid of is that while this matter is being taken care of with regard to London we will have the ambassadors extraordinary and ministers plenipotentiary at Tokyo and Washington stating that their services are worth more money than they are paid.
I think they are.

We have had very distinguished men occupying the office of High Commissioner at London tout it can never be said that the present High Commissioner has done more than Lord Strathcona did, and I never heard it suggested that more money should be offered to Lord Strathcona. I think the position should be an honorary one; but if it comes to the point where money is to be paid for these services, then let the matter be carefully weighed. This is one of the first positions under the government. It is well known that the office has been adorned by men who have been anxious to serve their country, and I am unwilling to see it put on a pecuniary basis. If an offer of $2,000 has been made, put it on a business basis and if necessary offer more.

Then why should it be
necessary for British subjects going from Canada to Great Britain to have passports before they are permitted to enter that country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That question has been asked repeatedly of the British government by our administration. The British government takes the position that they have adopted the passport regulations to enable them to control the admission of aliens. They contend that those who are British citizens will, in the long run, be occasioned less discomfort, if I may use that term, in their admission to Great Britain through having a passport than if they came without one. There is a process of examination which they desire to have in Great Britain in order to satisfy themselves as to persons not being aliens, and a passport apparently avoids any questioning. For that reason the British authorities have considered that plan as being preferable to having individuals undergo a course of examination and questioning on arrival. The matter has been taken up by correspondence, and it was taken up at the last imperial conference. If I am not mistaken, it was taken up at the previous imperial conference but the British government up to the present time has not seen fit to do away with the passport regulation.
The Prime Minister has said that this is done to make it easier for Canadians to enter Great Britain. I wonder if something could not be done to make it easier for Canadians to return to Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no
trouble getting back.

There is much more trouble
for a Canadian returning to Canada than there is for one going to Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
That has been my experience.

I have been told1 that there
is considerable delay in the passport office in the issuance of the passports. I do not know whether the complaints are all justified but some cases have come to my attention where the parties have been held up for three weeks without receiving a reply from the passport office. Some of these people had engaged a berth on a certain ship and had to use the telegraph to speed up the passport office in order to receive their passports in time. Would the Prime Minister look into this matter and see whether there is any unnecessary delay or whether the passport office is requiring information which perhaps is not necessary?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should be
veiy much obliged if the hon. member would give me the names of any persons who have

Supply-External Affairs
experienced delay in obtaining passports, and I will undertake to let him have a statement as to the date on which their applications were received and the date on which they were given their passports. I have heard from many sources that the passport office at Ottawa is particularly efficient and the government has been complimented over and over again on the fact that there is less delay and less red tape in the matter of getting a passport from the Canadian office than from any other. I think the information of the hon. member probably has been given to him in an exaggerated form, but I should like to look into it.

It is quite possible that the applicants may not have completed the form, or something of that kind. I have not the particulars, as these cases came to my attention when I was at home. Does the Prime Minister think unnecessary questions are being asked before a passport is granted, anid that the procedure is quite as simple as it might be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I am right in saying that the question of passports was taken up at the League of Nations with a view to having a similar set of questions asked in all countries. We have endeavoured to simplify our passports as much as possible and have brought the questions down to the minimum.

I think the hon. member for Macleod must be wrongly informed. I doubt if there is any other office where passports can be obtained as readily and with as courteous service as in this country. From my own personal experiences, one in Great Britain and one in France, I have come to the conclusion that we have nothing to learn in either promptness or courtesy in this regard. I think the difficulty arose through the correspondents of the hon. member having omitted to reply to what they thought to be an irrelevant question. Sometimes the signature is not put on the back of the photograph, and obviously that might give rise to a very difficult situation, because the country as such certifies to the validity of the passport, and with no signature there is nothing to indicate that the photograph is that of the person in question. If one is desirous of going to Great Britain the railway companies will take the requisite fee, have the form filled out and send the passport on to meet the passenger at the boat. I know of three cases since the opening of navigation this year in which that has been done. I only say that in justice to the gentlemen in charge of the office. One 78594-170
must speak of them as one finds them, and they have shown not for me alone, but for any person I have known who has had to communicate with them, a willingness to assist, a great courtesy, and an earnest desire to serve the public.

I think the trouble lies largely in the fact that the public do not understand the full information that is required of them with regard to passports. I am glad indeed to say that in any communications I have had with the passport office, I have been given the very best service. But I have had complaints from people who, not having the full information, have been wondering why their passports have been held up. That is where the trouble lies. The passport situation is a nuisance, but I am glad to say that I have received most excellent service from the passport office in Ottawa.

My experience has been the same; that is, 1 have received great courtesy, most efficient sendee and had the matter I was dealing with expedited as much as possible. But having many complaints with regard to delays that have taken place, just to see how long it really took, I followed step by step the case of a friend in my part of the country who was applying for a passport. Living, as many do, some distance from a railway, he received his mail by rural mail carrier twice a week. When he wrote me I went to the office and had the necessary form sent out to him, but it required about two weeks for his letter to reach Ottawa and for a reply to be sent. He wrote to Ottawa, and the application was promptly mailed to him, but this took two weeks. The application was sent back to Ottawa improperly filled out and had to be returned with explicit and courteous instructions as to what should be done. This took two more weeks. When he finally got the passport, a little over six weeks had elapsed, but almost the whole of that delay was due to the distance and the time required for the application to reach that outlying point and then to be returned. It took six weeks, without the slightest dilatoriness on the part of the passport office, the necessary information having been sent at the earliest possible moment.

So far as I have had any
communications with the passport office they have been answered as promptly as possible, but I have had cases where the time elapsing between the making of application for a passport and the receipt of it was just as long as in the instance quoted by the hon. member

for Red Deer. I am speaking only from memory, 'but in some cases it seems that an unnecessarily long time elapses between the despatch of a request for a passport and its being received. The delay may have been accounted for by circumstances which were not brought to my attention. Personally I have had the best service possible from the passport office.

As I understand the
matter, they deal with the applications in sequence.

I do not want in any
way to criticize or to sound a note of discord in regard to what has been said as to the work of the passport office. We are moving far away from the war and the post war period, and it seems to me that the work should therefore be lighter and easier. The sum of $5,500 is an important item. If an explanation were given why at this date the expenses of the office are increased, it might be illuminating.

Do I understand that our diplomatic representatives do not, except in cases of difficulty with the country to which they are accredited, deal with questions of trade and commerce and commercial matters?

speechtext: They deal with . all matters of governmental character.
I am speaking of-
Trade promotion?

Not only trade promotion, but questions connected with trade and commerce. I was advised, and I said that when I got the opportunity I would ascertain whether or not it is correct, that our diplomatic representatives do not deal with questions of trade except for the purpose of making representations. For instance, I assume that our representatives at Washington made representations with respect to the proposed new United States tariff, and that our diplomatic representative at Paris might make representations with respect to contemplated action by the government of France in connection with duties and matters of that kind. dividuals with respect to important trade matters in the countries to which they are accredited, and in creating the interest and affording .many of the facilities essential to the promotion of trade.

This question may come more pertinently under the next item, but perhaps the Geneva items will all be dealt with together. What check-up is there on the League of Nations in regard to its expenditure? I have seen a good deal of criticism in various sections of the press regarding the expenses of the league, and what appears to be everybody's business is nobody's business. That seems to be the impression of some of the English and Canadian journals that I have read. Would the Prime Minister give some explanation of how the expenses are checked?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals was on the budget committee at the last meeting of the League of Nations and can probably answer that question.

It is more difficult to get estimates past the budget committee of the League of Nations than past any legislative body of which I have been a member. The debates regarding what might be called the internal economy of the league and the presentation of the estimates for the various branches of the league's work certainly arouse very strong and very critical discussion. One can understand that when one remembers that some of the nations are not interested in certain phases of the league's work, and naturally they are very critical of expenditures on those phases which do not particularly interest them. The procedure is almost identical to that followed in this house. I can assure my bon. friend that I was surprised at the 
thoroughness with which the representatives of the various nations criticized the estimates and brought about from time to time reductions in the votes brought before the budget committee of the League of Nations.

I do not dispute that, but at the same time. I haye seen a good deal of criticism of the expenses of the league. 1 notice, for instance, that Canada's contribution, and we are one of the small countries of the world, is increased by over $21,000 this year. I am not trying to hold up the estimates of the Prime Minister, but he cannot get these four items relating to the league through to-night, so it does not really matter very much. It would be interesting to the committee if the Prime Minister when next these estimates are up would give a brief sketch of how the expenses of the League of Nations are made up and how our proportion is worked out. I do not expect anything lengthy.
